title: z-Domain System Analysis
description: Read stability, ringing and frequency response from the poles and zeros of H(z), and pick the right sequence with the region of convergence.

study.title: Transfer function
study.body: With all initial conditions zero, transform the difference equation term by term ($y[n-k] \to z^{-k}Y(z)$) and solve for $H(z) = Y(z)/X(z)$, the z-transform of the impulse response $h[n]$. Multiply numerator and denominator by $z^2$ to get positive powers. The feedback coefficients $a_k$ form the denominator. A causal system has a **proper** $H(z)$: numerator degree ≤ denominator degree.
study.formula: \begin{array}{c} y[n] + a_1y[n-1] + a_2y[n-2] \\ = b_0x[n] + b_1x[n-1] + b_2x[n-2] \\ \Downarrow \\ H(z) = \dfrac{b_0z^2 + b_1z + b_2}{z^2 + a_1z + a_2} \end{array}

study.title: Poles, zeros and stability
study.body: A causal system is BIBO stable when **all poles lie strictly inside the unit circle**. Simple poles on the circle make it marginally stable (a natural response that never dies out); any pole outside makes it unstable. Zeros do not affect stability, but a causal, stable **inverse** $1/H(z)$ needs all zeros inside the circle too.

study.title: Explore: pole radius and angle
study.body: A pole pair $re^{\pm j\Omega_p}$ gives an impulse response like $h[n] = r^n\cos(\Omega_p n)$. The **radius** sets the decay: the envelope $r^n$ falls by a factor $e$ every $-1/\ln r$ samples, so poles near the circle ring for a long time. The **angle** sets the oscillation: $2\pi/\Omega_p$ samples per cycle; at $\Omega_p = \pi$ the sign flips every sample.

study.title: Frequency response
study.body: Evaluate $H(z)$ on the unit circle, $z = e^{j\Omega}$ with $\Omega = \omega T$. Geometrically $|H|$ is the product of the distances from $e^{j\Omega}$ to the zeros, divided by the product of the distances to the poles: a pole near the circle gives a peak, a zero on it a null. $H(1)$ is the DC gain and $H(-1)$ the gain at $f_s/2$. A sinusoid $A\cos(\Omega_0n)$ leaves as $A|H(e^{j\Omega_0})|\cos(\Omega_0n + \angle H)$.

study.title: Explore: a resonator
study.body: $H(z) = \frac{z^2}{(z - re^{j\theta})(z - re^{-j\theta})}$ has a pole pair at angle $\theta$ and two zeros at the origin. As $r \to 1$ the poles approach the unit circle and the peak at $\Omega \approx \theta$ grows taller and narrower. The $-3$ dB width of the peak is about $2(1 - r)$ rad/sample.

study.title: Simple digital filters
study.body: The exponential smoother $y[n] = a\,y[n-1] + (1-a)\,x[n]$ is a first-order low-pass: pole at $a$, DC gain 1, gain $\frac{1-a}{1+a}$ at $\Omega = \pi$. A **notch** puts zeros exactly on the circle at $e^{\pm j\Omega_0}$, which removes that frequency completely; poles just inside at $re^{\pm j\Omega_0}$ keep the notch narrow and the gain near 1 elsewhere.

study.title: Bilateral z-transform and ROC
study.body: The bilateral transform sums over all $n$, and then $X(z)$ alone does not fix the sequence: the ROC does. Right-sided sequences converge **outside** the outermost pole, left-sided ones **inside** the innermost pole, two-sided ones in a **ring** between poles; the ROC never contains a pole. An LTI system is stable exactly when the ROC of $H(z)$ includes the unit circle.

steps.title: From difference equation to H(z)
steps.body: Set the initial conditions to zero and transform every term: a delay $y[n-k]$ becomes $z^{-k}Y(z)$. Collect $Y$ on the left and $X$ on the right. For example $y[n] - 0.5y[n-1] = x[n] + x[n-1]$ gives $Y(1 - 0.5z^{-1}) = X(1 + z^{-1})$.

ask.explanation: Transform: $Y(z)(1 - az^{-1}) = X(z)(b_0 + b_1z^{-1})$, so $H(z) = \frac{b_0z + b_1}{z - a}$. The pole is at $z = a$ = {{a}}.

steps.prompt:
Which difference equation has
$$H(z) = \frac{z + {{b}}}{z^2 - {{p}}z + {{q}}}?$$
steps.explanation: Divide numerator and denominator by $z^2$: $H = \frac{z^{-1} + {{b}}z^{-2}}{1 - {{p}}z^{-1} + {{q}}z^{-2}}$. Cross-multiplying gives $y[n] - {{p}}y[n-1] + {{q}}y[n-2] = x[n-1] + {{b}}x[n-2]$. The numerator degree is one less than the denominator, so the input enters with one sample of delay; the feedback terms change sign when moved to the right.

steps.title: Stability from the pole-zero map
steps.body: Each pole $p$ contributes a mode $p^n$ to the response. It dies out only if $|p| < 1$. So a causal system is **stable when every pole lies inside the unit circle**. Zeros (o) may lie anywhere; they shape the response but cannot make it grow.

steps.prompt: Which pole-zero map belongs to a **stable** causal system? (× pole, o zero, grey: unit circle)
steps.explanation: Only the first map has all poles inside the circle ($|0.5 \pm j0.6| = 0.78$); its zero on the circle is harmless. The pair $0.8 \pm j0.8$ has radius 1.13 (unstable), the pole at $z = 1$ is on the circle (marginally stable: the step-like mode never decays) and the pole at $-1.3$ gives a growing alternating mode.

steps.prompt:
The causal system
$$H(z) = \frac{z^2}{z^2 - {{p}}z + {{q}}}$$
is stable.
steps.explanation: Here $p^2 < 4q$, so the poles are a complex pair $re^{\pm j\Omega}$. Their product is $r^2$ = the constant term {{q}}, so $r = \sqrt{{{q}}}$ = {{sqrt(q)}}. Stable requires $r < 1$, i.e. a constant term below 1.

steps.title: Try it: pole radius and angle
steps.body: The dots show $h[n] = r^n\cos(\Omega_p n)$ for a pole pair at $re^{\pm j\Omega_p}$. Drag $r$ towards 1: the ringing lasts longer, and above 1 it grows. Drag the angle: small angles oscillate slowly, $\Omega_p = \pi$ flips the sign every sample.

steps.prompt: A system has a pole pair at $z$ = {{r}}$e^{\pm j\pi/{{kk}}}$.

ask.prompt: How many samples does one oscillation of the impulse response take?
ask.explanation: $N_{cycle} = 2\pi/\Omega_p = 2\pi/(\pi/{{kk}})$ = {{2*kk}} samples.

ask.prompt: After how many samples has the envelope $r^n$ dropped to 1 %?
ask.explanation: Solve $r^n = 0.01$: $n = \frac{\ln 0.01}{\ln r}$ = −4.61 / ln {{r}} = {{ln(0.01)/ln(r)}} samples. The closer the pole to the circle, the longer the ringing.

steps.prompt: Match each pole location to the impulse response it produces.
steps.explanation: A real pole $p$ gives $p^n$: decaying for $|p| < 1$, alternating for $p < 0$, constant for $p = 1$ and growing for $|p| > 1$. A complex pair $re^{\pm j\Omega}$ gives $r^n\cos(\Omega n + \theta)$: here a decaying oscillation with 8 samples per cycle.

steps.title: On the unit circle
steps.body: Set $z = e^{j\Omega}$ to get the frequency response. $|H|$ = (product of distances to the zeros) / (product of distances to the poles). Drag the pole pair of this resonator: the peak sits near the pole angle and sharpens as $r \to 1$. $H(1)$ gives the DC gain, $H(-1)$ the gain at $\Omega = \pi$.

steps.prompt:
The smoother $y[n] = {{a}}\,y[n-1] + {{1-a}}\,x[n]$ has
$$H(z) = \frac{{{1-a}}z}{z - {{a}}}$$
and its frequency response follows with $z = e^{j\Omega}$.

ask.explanation: $z = e^{j\pi} = -1$: $H(-1) = \frac{{{1-a}} \cdot (-1)}{-1 - {{a}}}$ = {{1-a}} / {{1+a}} = {{(1-a)/(1+a)}}. High frequencies are strongly attenuated.
$|e^{j\Omega}| = 1$, so $|H| = \frac{1-a}{|e^{j\Omega} - a|} = \frac{1-a}{\sqrt{1 - 2a\cos\Omega + a^2}}$ = {{1-a}} / $\sqrt{1 - 2 \cdot {{a}} \cdot {{cos(W)}} + {{a^2}}}$ = {{M}}.
$\angle H = \angle e^{j\Omega} - \angle(e^{j\Omega} - a) = \Omega - \mathrm{atan2}(\sin\Omega, \cos\Omega - a)$ = {{W*180/pi}}° − {{atan2(sin(W), cos(W)-a)*180/pi}}° = {{ph}}°: a phase lag.

steps.prompt: The FIR filter $y[n] = b_0x[n] + b_1x[n-1]$ with $b_0$ = {{b0}} and $b_1$ = {{b1}} gets the input $x[n] = {{A}}\cos(\pi n/{{kk}})$. Find the amplitude of the output.

$$H(z) = \frac{b_0z + b_1}{z - a}$$
with $b_0$ = {{b0}}, $b_1$ = {{b1}}, $a$ = {{a}}. Find the impulse response sample $h[{{N}}]$.
steps.explanation:
Split off the constant: $H(z) = b_0 + \frac{b_1 + ab_0}{z - a}$. The second term is $(b_1 + ab_0)\,z^{-1}\frac{z}{z-a}$, a delayed $a^n$. So $h[0] = b_0$ and $h[n] = (b_1 + ab_0)\,a^{n-1}$ for $n \geq 1$.
$h[{{N}}]$ = ({{b1}} + ({{a}}) × {{b0}}) × ({{a}})$^{{{N-1}}}$ = {{(b1 + a*b0)*a^(N-1)}}.

steps.prompt:
$y[n] = {{a}}\,y[n-1] + {{b}}\,x[n]$ with $y[-1]$ = {{y0}} gets a unit step $x[n] = u[n]$. Transforming gives
$$\begin{aligned} Y(z) &= \frac{{{a}}\,y[-1]\,z}{z - {{a}}} \\ &\quad {}+ \frac{{{b}}\,z^2}{(z - {{a}})(z - 1)} \end{aligned}$$
Invert it term by term.

ask.explanation:
The first term is the zero-input response: $a\,y[-1]\,a^n = y[-1]\,a^{n+1}$.
At $n$ = {{N}}: {{y0}} × {{a}}$^{{{N+1}}}$ = {{zi}}.

Zero-input: $y[-1]a^{n+1}$ = {{zi}}. Zero-state (partial fractions of the second term): $b\,\frac{1 - a^{n+1}}{1 - a}$ = {{zs}}.
Total: {{zi}} + {{zs}} = {{zi + zs}}.
The initial condition dies out ($|a| < 1$). What remains is the DC gain times the step: $H(1) = \frac{b}{1 - a}$ = {{b}} / {{1-a}} = {{b/(1-a)}}.

steps.prompt:
A system has
$$H(z) = \frac{{{K}}(z + {{c}})}{z^2 - {{p}}z + {{q}}}$$
with both poles inside the unit circle (stable).

ask.prompt: A step of height {{A}} is applied. Find the final value of the output.
ask.explanation:
In steady state a constant input is multiplied by the DC gain $H(1)$ = {{K}} × {{1+c}} / (1 − {{p}} + {{q}}) = {{K*(1+c)/(1-p+q)}}.
Output: {{A}} × {{K*(1+c)/(1-p+q)}} = {{A*K*(1+c)/(1-p+q)}}.

ask.prompt: The input is $x[n] = {{A}}(-1)^n$. Find the steady-state output $y[n]$ at even $n$.

steps.prompt: A resonator with poles 0.95$e^{\pm j\theta}$ runs at $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}}. Set the pole angle $\theta$ so the peak lies at $f_0$ = {{f0|Hz}}.
steps.explanation: The peak sits at $\Omega \approx \theta$ (exactly for $r \to 1$). Convert the frequency: $\theta = \Omega_0 = 2\pi f_0/f_s$ = 2π × {{f0}} / {{fs}} = {{2*pi*f0/fs}} rad.

steps.prompt: A notch filter must remove {{f0}} Hz hum from a signal sampled at {{fs|Hz}}. Its zeros sit on the unit circle at $e^{\pm j\Omega_0}$, so its numerator is $z^2 + b_1z + 1$.

ask.explanation: $\Omega_0 = 2\pi f_0/f_s$ = 2π × {{f0}} / {{fs}} = {{W0}} rad/sample.
$(z - e^{j\Omega_0})(z - e^{-j\Omega_0}) = z^2 - 2z\cos\Omega_0 + 1$. With $\Omega_0$ = 2π × {{f0}}/{{fs}} = {{W0}} rad: $b_1 = -2\cos\Omega_0$ = {{-2*cos(W0)}}.

steps.prompt: Choose $a$ in $y[n] = a\,y[n-1] + (1-a)\,x[n]$ so the filter mimics an RC low-pass with $\tau$ = {{tau|s}} at $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}}. (Map the pole with $z = e^{sT}$; give 4 decimals.)
steps.explanation:
The RC pole is $s = -1/\tau$, which maps to $a = e^{-T/\tau}$ with $T = 1/f_s$ = {{1/fs|s}}.
$a = e^{-{{1/fs}}/{{tau}}}$ = $e^{-{{1/(fs*tau)}}}$ = {{exp(-1/(fs*tau))||5}}.
The shortcut $a \approx 1 - T/\tau$ = {{1-1/(fs*tau)||5}} is only close when $\tau$ spans many samples (here {{fs*tau}}).

steps.prompt:
$$H(z) = \frac{z - c}{z - 0.5}$$
with $c$ = {{c}} has a stable, causal inverse system.
steps.explanation: The inverse is $H^{-1}(z) = \frac{z - 0.5}{z - c}$: the zeros of $H$ become its poles. It is stable and causal only if the zero $c$ lies inside the unit circle. Here $|c|$ = {{abs(c)}}.

steps.title: The bilateral transform needs an ROC
steps.body: Summing over all $n$, both $a^nu[n]$ and $-a^nu[-n-1]$ give $\frac{z}{z-a}$: the first converges for $|z| > |a|$, the second for $|z| < |a|$. So with the bilateral transform always state the ROC. Right-sided: outside the outermost pole; left-sided: inside the innermost pole; two-sided: a ring between poles.

steps.prompt:
$$X(z) = \frac{z}{z - {{a}}}$$
with ROC $|z| <$ {{a}}. Which sequence is $x[n]$?
steps.explanation: An ROC inside the pole means a left-sided sequence. $\sum_{n=-\infty}^{-1} -a^nz^{-n} = -\sum_{m\geq1}(z/a)^m = \frac{z}{z-a}$ for $|z| < |a|$. The causal $a^nu[n]$ has the same formula but the ROC $|z| > |a|$.

ask.explanation: The ROC lies outside the pole {{p1}} (right-sided term $({{p1}})^nu[n]$) and inside the pole {{p2}} (left-sided term $-({{p2}})^nu[-n-1]$). For $n \geq 0$ only the first counts: $x[{{N}}]$ = {{p1}}$^{{{N}}}$ = {{p1^N}}.
For $n < 0$ only the left-sided term $-({{p2}})^nu[-n-1]$ is nonzero: $x[-{{N}}]$ = −{{p2}}$^{-{{N}}}$ = {{-p2^(-N)}}.

steps.prompt: Match each sequence or property to its region of convergence.
steps.explanation: Each pole sets a boundary of the ROC; the ROC itself never contains a pole. Causal (right-sided) systems converge outside, anti-causal ones inside, two-sided ones in between. Stability means $\sum|h[n]|$ converges, which is the ROC including $|z| = 1$.

steps.prompt: An LTI system with poles at {{p1}} and {{p2}} can be stable if it does not have to be causal.
steps.explanation: Choose the ROC {{p1}} $< |z| <$ {{p2}}: it contains the unit circle, so the system is stable. The impulse response is then two-sided (the pole at {{p2}} gives a left-sided term), so the system is not causal. A causal version would need $|z| >$ {{p2}} and be unstable.

steps.prompt: A system obeys $y[n] = {{p}}\,y[n-1] - {{q}}\,y[n-2] + x[n]$.

ask.prompt: Find the radius of its poles.
ask.explanation: $H(z) = \frac{z^2}{z^2 - {{p}}z + {{q}}}$. For a complex pair $re^{\pm j\Omega}$ the denominator is $z^2 - 2r\cos\Omega\,z + r^2$, so $r = \sqrt{{{q}}}$ = {{r}}: stable.

ask.prompt: Find the pole angle $\Omega$ in rad/sample.
ask.explanation: $r = \sqrt{{{q}}}$ = {{r}} and $2r\cos\Omega$ = {{p}}, so $\cos\Omega$ = {{p}} / (2 × {{r}}) = {{cos(W)}} and $\Omega$ = {{W}} rad.

ask.prompt: How many samples does one cycle of its ringing take?
ask.explanation: $\cos\Omega = \frac{{{p}}}{2\sqrt{{{q}}}}$ = {{cos(W)}}, $\Omega$ = {{W}} rad, so $N_{cycle} = 2\pi/\Omega$ = {{2*pi/W}} samples.

steps.prompt:
A resonator has
$$H(z) = \frac{z^2}{z^2 - {{c||4}}z + {{r^2||4}}},$$
poles $re^{\pm j\theta}$.

ask.prompt: Find the gain $|H(e^{j\theta})|$ at the pole angle.
ask.explanation:
$r = \sqrt{{{r^2||4}}}$ = {{r}}, $\cos\theta$ = {{c||4}}/(2r) = {{cos(th)}}, so $\theta$ = π/{{kk}}. Distances from $e^{j\theta}$: to the zeros at 0: 1 each; to the near pole $re^{j\theta}$: $1 - r$ = {{1-r}}; to the far pole $re^{-j\theta}$: $\sqrt{1 - 2r\cos 2\theta + r^2}$ = {{sqrt(1 - 2*r*cos(2*th) + r^2)}}.
$|H|$ = 1 / ({{1-r}} × {{sqrt(1 - 2*r*cos(2*th) + r^2)}}) = {{1/((1-r)*sqrt(1 - 2*r*cos(2*th) + r^2))}}.

steps.prompt: $x[n] = \cos(\pi n/2)$ drives $y[n] = {{a}}\,y[n-1] + {{1-a}}\,x[n]$. In steady state $y[n] = |H|\cos(\pi n/2 + \angle H)$ with $H = H(e^{j\pi/2}) = H(j)$.

ask.explanation:
$H(j) = \frac{(1-a)\,j}{j - a}$. Multiply by the conjugate $(-j - a)$: $H(j) = \frac{(1-a)(1 - ja)}{1 + a^2}$.
$y[0] = |H|\cos\angle H = \mathrm{Re}\,H$ = {{1-a}} / {{1+a^2}} = {{(1-a)/(1+a^2)}}.

steps.prompt: Which filter removes $\Omega_0 = \pi/{{kk}}$ **completely** while keeping the gain close to 1 at other frequencies, and is stable?
steps.explanation: A complete null needs zeros **on** the unit circle at $e^{\pm j\pi/{{kk}}}$: $z^2 - 2\cos(\pi/{{kk}})z + 1$ = $z^2 - {{c||4}}z + 1$. Poles at $0.9e^{\pm j\pi/{{kk}}}$ (inside) narrow the notch. Swapping them puts poles on the circle (not stable); zeros at radius 0.9 only dip; the $+$ signs place the notch at $\pi - \Omega_0$.

steps.prompt:
A **stable** LTI system has
$$H(z) = \frac{z}{z - a} + \frac{z}{z - b}$$
with $a$ = {{a}} and $b$ = {{b}}.

ask.explanation: Stable means the ROC contains $|z| = 1$: {{abs(a)}} $< |z| <$ {{abs(b)}}. So $\frac{z}{z-a} \to a^nu[n]$ (right-sided) and $\frac{z}{z-b} \to -b^nu[-n-1]$ (left-sided). For $n \geq 0$: $h[{{N}}]$ = ({{a}})$^{{{N}}}$ = {{a^N}}.
The ROC {{abs(a)}} $< |z| <$ {{abs(b)}} contains the unit circle, so the pole at {{b}} contributes the left-sided term $-b^nu[-n-1]$. $h[-{{N}}]$ = −({{b}})$^{-{{N}}}$ = {{-b^(-N)}}.

steps.prompt:
An echo channel
$$H(z) = \frac{z - c}{z - a}$$
with $c$ = {{c}}, $a$ = {{a}} is undone by the inverse $G(z) = 1/H(z)$. Find $g[{{N}}]$, a sample of its impulse response.
steps.explanation:
$G(z) = \frac{z - a}{z - c} = 1 + \frac{c - a}{z - c}$, stable and causal because $|c| < 1$. The second term is $(c - a)\,z^{-1}\frac{z}{z-c}$, so $g[n] = (c - a)\,c^{n-1}$ for $n \geq 1$.
$g[{{N}}]$ = ({{c}} − {{a}}) × ({{c}})$^{{{N-1}}}$ = {{(c-a)*c^(N-1)}}.
